#12944. The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1966 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Establishing a permanent human presence on the Moon will require more than rockets, habitats, and life support systems.
  • Recent findings suggest that materials used in lunar construction must also survive transportation, installation, accidental impacts, and years of handling.
  • Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania may have found an answer in an unexpectedly familiar material: Mylar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Establishing a permanent human presence on the Moon will require more than rockets, habitats, and life support systems. Engineers must also find ways to protect astronauts and equipment from extreme temperatures that can swing from hundreds of degrees below zero to boiling hot. Reliable insulation will be essential, but keeping heat under control is only part of the problem.

Recent findings suggest that materials used in lunar construction must also survive transportation, installation, accidental impacts, and years of handling. Many of the best insulators are surprisingly delicate, making them poorly suited to the demanding conditions of a working Moon base.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania may have found an answer in an unexpectedly familiar material: Mylar. This lightweight plastic is used in everyday products such as food wrap and, when coated with aluminum, the reflective emergency blankets that help marathon runners retain body heat. By arranging hundreds of extremely thin Mylar sheets into carefully designed stacks, the team has created insulation that remains effective even after being bent or subjected to intense pressure.

Recent findings suggest that the research, published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, introduces a material known as hybrid layered insulating film stacks (HyLIFS). Its main advantage is the ability to combine two qualities that are difficult to achieve together: excellent thermal insulation and resistance to physical damage.

"These stacks of Mylar can bend, withstand substantial compression and maintain their insulating performance," notes senior author Igor Bargatin, Associate Professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM), "potentially allowing them to be packed, transported and survive rough treatment over many years of use.".

If engineers can eventually manufacture the material on a large scale, it could be used to protect lunar habitats, spacesuits, and other equipment designed to function for extended periods in the vacuum of space.

"The combination of thermal and mechanical robustness is critical for long-term use on the Moon," notes first author Danielle R. Levin, a recent Penn doctoral graduate in chemistry, who also received a master's in MEAM. "This material could open a pathway to inexpensive, durable and reusable lunar insulation.".

Why Moon Bases Need Tougher Insulation.

According to recent reports, designing insulation for the Moon involves a difficult balancing act. A material must slow the movement of heat through a vacuum while also remaining strong enough to withstand the stresses of everyday use.

It has been revealed that some existing materials are outstanding at preventing heat transfer but offer little protection against physical damage. Aerogels, for instance, consist mostly of empty space, which makes them extremely lightweight and effective at retaining heat. They have been used in applications ranging from industrial pipelines to NASA's Mars rovers. However, their delicate internal structure can make them vulnerable to impacts and compression.

According to recent reports, another widely used space technology, multilayer insulation, relies on reflective sheets separated by insulating spacers. It works particularly well at reducing heat transfer through radiation, but it is not intended to support substantial weight. Even routine contact can cause tearing or other damage.

Sources indicate that strengthening insulation often creates another problem: the changes that make it more durable can also allow more heat to pass through. For future lunar infrastructure, engineers need a material that can resist damage without sacrificing thermal performance.

"For lunar infrastructure, we would ideally like both," notes Bargatin. "The ideal material is both resistant to damage and to the loss of heat.".

How Ordinary Mylar Became Powerful Space Insulation.

According to recent reports, the Penn researchers focused on Mylar, a well-known plastic formally called biaxially oriented polyethylene terephthalate, or BoPET. Already used extensively in aerospace technology, the polymer is also found in the lightweight emergency blankets distributed after marathons. Adding a metallic coating such as aluminum allows Mylar to reflect infrared radiation, helping prevent heat from escaping.

Rather than relying on a single sheet, the researchers investigated what would happen if many thin layers were stacked together. They experimented with different film thicknesses and applied extremely thin coatings of aluminum oxide, also called alumina, to some samples to make the sheets stiffer.

Assembling the experimental stacks was surprisingly difficult. Each delicate film had to be positioned individually, requiring painstaking manual work.

"At the moment, the process is very time-consuming," notes Levin. "We use two pairs of tweezers and small weights to handle and stack the delicate films. Even breathing near the stack can send the layers flying.".

Recent findings suggest that despite the simplicity of the basic idea, testing revealed an impressive combination of properties. In a vacuum, the best stacks achieved thermal conductivity comparable to other advanced vacuum insulation materials while retaining their flexibility.

The researchers also tested the material under compression similar to what insulation could experience inside a lunar habitat, where the interior air pressure would push against walls exposed to the vacuum outside.

In a recent development, additional mechanical testing indicated that stacks coated with alumina could tolerate the greatest compressive stresses available with the laboratory equipment while maintaining their insulating performance. The results demonstrated that improving durability did not necessarily require giving up thermal protection.

Crushing Pressure Reveals Unexpected Durability.

Sources indicate that one of the most striking findings came when the team subjected the material to repeated compression. Even the researchers were surprised by how well the thin plastic layers held up.

The samples were compressed to approximately 20 megapascals, a pressure comparable to concentrating 200 pounds of force onto an area the size of a fingertip. Instead of testing the material only once, the researchers repeated the process 10 times.

In a recent development, "We were concerned about the material failing under such high compressive stress," recalls Levin. "But the stacks didn't survive just one high stress cycle -- they survived 10 in a row.".

Industry observers note that this resistance to damage could be especially valuable for lunar exploration. Every piece of equipment needed on the Moon must first endure the challenges of being packed, launched, transported, and installed. Insulation that can bend, withstand pressure, and potentially be reused would offer significant practical advantages.

Durability would remain vital after construction is complete. Astronauts living and working inside a lunar habitat could accidentally strike or compress insulation during maintenance or ordinary activities.

"You could use these stacks to insulate a lunar habitation, but astronauts will inevitably have little accidents where they bump into them," notes Bargatin. "When we're talking about long-term habitation on the moon, it's really important to have tough materials that can last long enough.".

Tiny Particles Reveal a Hidden Secret of Heat Transfer.

Beyond demonstrating the material's durability, the experiments uncovered an key clue about how heat travels through layers of Mylar.

Industry observers note that the discovery involved microscopic particles already present in commercially manufactured plastic films. Extremely thin sheets naturally tend to stick to one another and to nearby surfaces, which complicates manufacturing and handling. To prevent this, producers add tiny "antiblocking" particles that extend slightly above the plastic surface and keep neighboring sheets from clinging together.

Although manufacturers have long understood why these particles are useful, their influence on heat transfer in stacked Mylar films had received relatively little attention.

Industry observers note that traditional multilayer space insulation is primarily designed to control heat transferred by radiation. As a result, researchers have had less reason to investigate how small points of physical contact between films might affect heat conduction.

The Penn team examined this possibility by constructing mathematical models of heat transfer between individual layers and comparing the predictions with laboratory measurements.

The findings indicate that, in a vacuum, much of the heat moving from one Mylar sheet to the next passes through the tiny contact points created by the antiblocking particles.

That result could have notable implications for future insulation design. Instead of accepting the particles as an incidental feature of commercial plastic, engineers might deliberately control their size, abundance, and placement to reduce unwanted heat transfer.

Why Thinner Plastic Does Not Always Insulate Better.

The role of these microscopic particles also helped explain another unexpected result.

In a recent development, at first, the researchers assumed that thinner Mylar sheets would produce better insulation. Using thinner films would allow more layers to occupy the same amount of space, increasing the number of boundaries that heat must cross.

However, the experiments did not fully support that expectation. When coated with alumina, the thinnest films the team successfully characterized provided thermal performance similar to films of medium thickness.

The researchers suspect that the antiblocking particles help explain why. In thinner sheets, the particles can produce more contact between adjacent layers, creating additional routes for heat to move through the material. Those extra contact points can offset the expected advantages of adding more layers.

The finding suggests that making films thinner is not automatically the best approach. Engineers must also consider how the sheets bend and deform under pressure, along with the number and arrangement of microscopic contact points.

"As you compress the layers, the contact landscape changes," states Levin. "It's not just a matter of minimizing the film thickness or the number of particles; we must also account for how the contacts change and the films deform as pressure increases.".

Ultimately, the ability of these stacks to limit heat transfer depends on several interacting factors, including the thickness and stiffness of the plastic and the distribution of particles within it.

From Tiny Laboratory Samples to Future Moon Bases.

Although the early results are encouraging, the new insulation is still far from being ready for lunar construction.

The experimental HyLIFS samples presently measure only about one square centimeter, and producing them requires hours of careful cutting and manual stacking. That painstaking process would be impractical for manufacturing the large sheets needed to insulate an entire habitat.

It has been revealed that to make the material useful on a larger scale, the researchers will need a more efficient production method. One possibility involves continuously applying coatings to large rolls of Mylar, using manufacturing techniques that could eventually produce sheets measured in meters rather than centimeters.

Such an approach might also allow engineers to adjust the thickness of the plastic, the protective coatings, and the distribution of antiblocking particles before assembling the material into larger stacks.

Industry observers note that notable questions remain. The researchers still need to determine whether large versions of the material will retain the same insulating properties and mechanical strength seen in the laboratory. Further testing must also establish how well the stacks tolerate repeated bending, accidental impacts, scratches, and other wear associated with real-world use.

If those challenges can be overcome, the technology could provide lightweight, flexible, durable insulation for lunar habitats, rovers, electronic equipment, and other systems operating in space.

In a recent development, for Levin, the results also offer a broader lesson about materials engineering. Even familiar products can reveal unexpected capabilities when researchers examine how their structures behave under different conditions.

"The simplest configuration ended up being the best one," she says.

The research was carried out at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science (Penn Engineering). Additional co-authors include Matthew F. Campbell, Gulzhan Aldan, and Orevaoghene H. Omodior.

Funding was provided by the National Science Foundation Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems (grant number 1845933) and Penn Engineering.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission has begun its journey home to Earth.

In a recent development, the robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) today at 12:05 p.m. EST (1705 GMT), while the duo were flying 260 miles (418 kilometers) above western China.

According to recent reports, if all goes according to blueprint, the freighter will splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov. 21) at about 4:55 p.m. EST (2155 GMT). There will be no livestream for its reentry and splashdown. (Today's departure webcast did not feature live footage of the moment of undocking, as it occurred during a gap in coverage of the high-bandwidth signal needed for video.).

It has been revealed that the Dragon released Oct. 13, on a mission called CRS-35 because it's the 35th that SpaceX has flown for NASA's Commercial Resupply Services program.

Industry observers note that the capsule arrived at the ISS on Oct. 15, delivering more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of food, scientific gear and other supplies to the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. It will bring a lot of stuff down to Earth, too.

Industry observers note that "Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth," NASA officials wrote in an patch on Tuesday (Nov. 17).

"The returning research includes a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct scientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth," they added.

Dragon is the only cargo craft flying today that's capable of making such downward deliveries. The others — Northrop Grumman's Cygnus, Russia's Progress vehicle and Japan's HTV-X — are all expendable and burn up in Earth's atmosphere to wrap up their first and only spaceflight.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:20 p.m. ET on Nov. 20 with news of successful undocking.

Twitter’s traditional bird icon was booted and replaced with an image of a Shiba Inu, an apparent nod to dogecoin, the joke cryptocurrency that CEO Elon Musk is being sued over.

Musk addressed the change Monday afternoon, tweeting, “as promised” above an image of a year-old conversation in which another user suggested that Musk “just buy Twitter” and “change the bird logo to a doge.”.

According to recent reports, elon Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out one account.

The doge logo appeared on the site two days after Musk asked a judge to throw out a $258 billion racketeering lawsuit accusing him of running a pyramid scheme to support the dogecoin, according to Reuters.

Lawyers for Musk and Tesla called the lawsuit by dogecoin investors a “fanciful work of fiction” over Musk’s “innocuous and often silly tweets.”.

Sources indicate that it wasn’t clear whether the logo change was permanent. Musk has been known to use Twitter to troll both his fans and his critics.

The price of dogecoin, which is typically volatile, was up more than 20% over the past 24 hours, to about 9 cents. It was trading just under 8 cents Monday morning.

Dogecoin was created December 6, 2013, by a pair of software engineers — as a joke. The name is a nod to the “doge” meme that became popular a decade ago. Its Shiba Inu mascot mimicks that meme: a dog surrounded by a bunch of Comic Sans text in broken English.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JPMorgan Chase reported a "technical matter" that was affecting some consumer banking services Monday.

The bank noted a "temporary matter related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" was causing some customer transactions to take longer than usual, though it said customers can still access their accounts and funds.

"There is no evidence it is cyber-related," a JPMorgan spokesperson noted in a statement to CNBC.

"This is not a systemic matter — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," the spokesperson said. "We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today.".

CNBC's Eamon Javers reported there was no indication of bad actors involved.

In a recent development, still, other major banks were listed in outage reports as transactions between Chase and other institutions appeared to get held up. People reported errors as early as 11:30 a.m. ET.

A representative for U.S. Bank said that organization was "not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.".

Zelle is the peer-to-peer payments system backed by many of the largest U.S. banks, including JPMorgan.

The outage reports come days after separate, widespread challenges with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers.

— CNBC's Leslie Picker contributed to this report.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal.
  • To investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal.
  • Sources indicate that the experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. Known as a heavy fermion state, this phenomenon causes electrons to behave as though they have much greater mass than normal. These states are associated with extraordinary quantum effects, including unconventional superconductivity, and the discovery could provide a upcoming way to develop materials with unusual electronic properties.

To investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used powerful synchrotron light to study the electrons and their interactions at the boundary between the two materials. The results indicated that electrons confined to the thin atomic layer could interact with freely moving electrons in the copper beneath it, producing the unusual heavy fermion behavior.

Two Distinct Quantum States Emerge.

Sources indicate that the experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics. One existed primarily within the two-dimensional atomic layer, while the other reached beyond that layer and into the three-dimensional copper crystal below.

In a recent development, the second state was particularly key because it provided the first direct evidence of heavy fermion behavior generated by interactions across such an interface. Researchers traced the effect to the mixing, or hybridization, of localized ytterbium 4f electrons in the atomic layer with mobile conduction electrons inside the copper substrate. This interaction demonstrated how combining materials with different electronic characteristics can produce quantum behavior that neither material would necessarily exhibit on its own.

"This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible," claims senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. "Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity.".

A Latest Approach to Designing Quantum Materials.

The discovery suggests that the boundaries between materials could become powerful tools for creating and controlling exotic quantum states. Rather than relying only on the properties of individual substances, scientists may be able to develop entirely newly introduced electronic behaviors by carefully selecting and combining ultrathin atomic layers with suitable underlying materials.

Future research could focus on adjusting the structures of these interfaces, controlling the electronic orbitals involved, and manipulating moiré patterns that arise when atomic arrangements overlap. Such approaches may allow researchers to produce and fine-tune quantum phenomena in materials with extremely small dimensions, including effects that cannot be achieved in conventional materials. Ultimately, this could open new possibilities for engineering advanced quantum materials and investigating unconventional superconductivity.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is ready for battle in its opening weekend at the box office.

It has been revealed that the sixth film in the Lionsgate franchise grossed $21 million in Thursday previews before hitting 4,018 North American theaters on Friday. This gives it the second-best previews figure for the franchise, behind only the $25.2 million that 2013’s The Hunger Games: Catching Fire collected and besting the $19.7 million that the original Jennifer Lawrence-led film The Hunger Games earned when launching the franchise in 2012. Industry observers note that lionsgate had projected The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping to gross north of $80 million, but other sources expected that it would open much higher and potentially earn between $100 million and $130 million, which now appears the more likely outcome. Adapting author Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel that was published last year, director Francis Lawrence‘s movie carries a production budget of roughly $150 million as it revitalizes the franchise in telling a story set 24 years before the events of the original 2008 book.

It has been revealed that in the new film, Joseph Zada stars Haymitch Abernathy, providing the backstory for the character whom Woody Harrelson brought to life in the first four movies. The cast for Sunrise on the Reaping also includes Mckenna Grace, Whitney Peak, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Elle Fanning, Kieran Culkin and Maya Hawke.

The Hunger Games franchise’s five films have surpassed $3.3 billion at the global box office, with the series coming off of its lowest-performing entry with 2023 prequel The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. #12935. Everything about BepiColombo entering Mercury orbit on Saturday

Everything about BepiColombo entering Mercury orbit on Saturday

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (833 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A robotic spacecraft that has spent eight years looping around the inner solar system is finally set to lock into orbit around Mercury, the planet closest to the sun.
  • In a recent development, the European-Japanese mission, called BepiColombo, carries two science probes stacked on top of each other.
  • Recent findings suggest that A significant engine burn should steer the pair into a regular, closed orbit that passes over the planet's north and south poles on Saturday, Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A robotic spacecraft that has spent eight years looping around the inner solar system is finally set to lock into orbit around Mercury, the planet closest to the sun.

In a recent development, the European-Japanese mission, called BepiColombo, carries two science probes stacked on top of each other. One is the European Space Agency's Mercury Planetary Orbiter, or MPO. The other is Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, nicknamed Mio.

Recent findings suggest that A significant engine burn should steer the pair into a regular, closed orbit that passes over the planet's north and south poles on Saturday, Nov. 21.

In a recent development, mercury is the least explored planet in the inner solar system. Only two spacecraft have ever visited it, NASA's Mariner 10 in the 1970s and Messenger in the 2010s. That will make BepiColombo just the second mission to orbit Mercury and the first to put two orbiters there at once. One probe will observe the planet itself and the other will study its space environment. Scientists hope the results will show how rocky planets like Earth form and change when they're born close to their star.

According to recent reports, reaching Mercury is actually harder than getting to Pluto. Falling toward the sun isn't the only problem. It's bleeding off enough energy to avoid overshooting the planet.

Recent findings suggest that bepiColombo launched on Oct. 20, 2018, on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou, French Guiana. For most of the trip, it rode on a separate engine module that used ion thrusters. These engines push the spacecraft by firing charged particles out the back. The force was about as strong as the weight of two sheets of paper resting on your hand. But the thrusters ran for two years, carrying the spacecraft about 6 billion miles.

According to recent reports, the spacecraft also used gravity from nearby planets to bend its path. It swung past Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times. In Sep. 2024, it passed within about 100 miles of Mercury, the closest any spacecraft has ever flown past a planet. The trip wasn't smooth sailing. The engine module's solar panels started losing power, so the team had to slow down and push back the arrival date. Controllers detached the engine module on Sep. 3.

"It's a very difficult mission and very challenging because we are flying into a very, very harsh environment," Bruno Sousa, ESA's head of operations definition and engineering, mentioned during a livestream that day. Mercury's surface can drop below -290 degrees Fahrenheit at night and climb above 750 degrees during the day. The spacecraft gets baked from two sides — by sunlight and heat rising off the planet.

The arrival itself is unusual. Most missions hit the brakes hard and drop straight into orbit. BepiColombo is coming in slowly instead, and it gets there in steps. First, it drifts into Mercury's gravitational grip on a loose, irregular path that doesn't loop all the way around the planet. Engineers call this "weak capture." Spacecraft operations manager Ignacio "Nacho" Clérigo remarked no one has tried it with a planet before, only with moons. Saturday's big burn swaps that wandering path for a true orbit. It starts out as a long, lopsided oval, and the spacecraft fires its engines about every three days to reel it in.

It has been revealed that as the orbit tightens, a series of handoffs follow. On Dec. 9 and 10, the European orbiter releases Mio into its final orbit. Full science work should begin in April 2027.

In a recent development, mercury holds plenty of puzzles. It's unusually heavy for its size. Apart from Earth, it's the only rocky planet with a magnetic field surrounding the whole planet. Scientists want to learn whether Mercury's huge liquid core has a solid center. Others blueprint to measure magnesium, potassium, and calcium in the space around Mercury. Those elements offer indirect clues about what the surface is made of.

It has been revealed that the mission is named for Italian mathematician and engineer Giuseppe "Bepi" Colombo. His work on using planets' gravity to steer spacecraft helped make the earlier Mercury missions possible as well as BepiColombo's long, looping route.

Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, an eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function.
  • The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, an eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.

The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.

These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.

To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills.

One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn fresh things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.

The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.

Sources indicate that "The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently.

The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.

Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.

According to recent reports, working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing newly introduced information.

Sources indicate that light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.

The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.

Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity.

The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.

Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.

Sources indicate that one possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.

This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is crucial to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing.".

What the Eight-Year Study Revealed.

The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.

Industry observers note that the current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.

Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.

Recent findings suggest that to evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.

Industry observers note that importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.

Nevertheless, the results offer an crucial perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.

The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.

Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.

The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Drama is a comedy — or so say the backers of the film, about an engaged couple’s darkest secrets, in their submission for the Golden Globes, which requires all films be entered as either A) a drama or B) a musical or a comedy.
  • Other comedy entries include I Play Rocky, about the making of Rocky (which competed at the Globes as a drama); Obsession, about a young woman’s loss of agency; Tender Loving Care, about the frustrations of two young women, including the decline of one’s father; Artificial, about AI growing out of control; and Project Hail Mary, about a man sent into space against his will to try to stave off the end of the world.
  • Yes, all of the aforementioned musical/comedy submissions have moments of laughter and all of the dramas have elements of drama — but still, these classifications are pretty eyebrow-raising, begging the questions: What is going on?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Drama is a comedy — or so say the backers of the film, about an engaged couple’s darkest secrets, in their submission for the Golden Globes, which requires all films be entered as either A) a drama or B) a musical or a comedy. And that’s not even one of this year’s more questionable submissions.

Other comedy entries include I Play Rocky, about the making of Rocky (which competed at the Globes as a drama); Obsession, about a young woman’s loss of agency; Tender Loving Care, about the frustrations of two young women, including the decline of one’s father; Artificial, about AI growing out of control; and Project Hail Mary, about a man sent into space against his will to try to stave off the end of the world. Meanwhile, Club Kid, about a man-child who ends up with a child — widely described as an elevated version of Adam Sandler’s comedy Significant Daddy — has been entered as a drama. Related Stories Movies IDFA: 'The Year of the Ghost' and 'Memories of Lightning' Win Amsterdam Doc Fest Awards TV CBS Inks Newly introduced Deal to Air Kennedy Center Honors.

Yes, all of the aforementioned musical/comedy submissions have moments of laughter and all of the dramas have elements of drama — but still, these classifications are pretty eyebrow-raising, begging the questions: What is going on? And is there a better way?

The first Globes were held in 1944. There were no genre-specific Globes categories until the eighth, when the lead acting categories were split into two, one for dramas, the other for musicals/comedies. The following year, the same split was implemented for best picture. That category was reunified for the 11th ceremony, but the split was brought back for the 12th and every year since, helping to attract more stars to the ceremony.

Until 2023, Globes category submissions were made by studios and reviewed by the HFPA’s reminders list committee, which rarely overturned anything, even as dramas with music passed as musicals (Ray, Walk the Line and Rocketman), dramas with few laughs passed as comedies (Ghost, The Tourist and My Week With Marilyn) and comedies passed as dramas (All About Eve, Born Yesterday, Harvey and Sunset Boulevard — all in the same year). Once in a blue moon, the committee would reject a submission (Promising Young Woman as a musical/comedy), but it usually deferred to studios’ preferences.

In a recent development, frustrations burst into the open in 2015 after The Martian, a film about an astronaut stranded on Mars, was submitted and accepted as a musical/comedy. Judd Apatow, whose comedy Trainwreck was in contention that year, tweeted, “Trying to dominate the comedy category when you are really a drama afraid of dramatic competition is a punk move.” The Martian ended up beating Trainwreck for best picture, something Apatow was still smarting over when he presented at this year’s Globes: “My film Trainwreck lost best comedy to Ridley Scott’s The Martian. You know Ridley Scott, America’s favorite comedy director — director of such hilarious comedies as Gladiator, Blade Runner and Alien? I can’t wait till later tonight when best comedy is won by Hamnet.”.

According to recent reports, but ownership of the Globes had changed in 2023 (the Globes now share the same owners as THR), resulting in widespread reforms. This year’s rules declare: “Motion pictures shall be entered in the category that best matches the overall intent, tone and content of the film. Therefore, a motion picture that is primarily intended to have a serious or dramatic tone but contains comedic overtones or elements shall be entered as a drama as opposed to a comedy. Likewise, a motion picture that is primarily intended to have a comedic or satirical tone but contains dramatic overtones or elements shall be entered as a comedy as opposed to a drama.”.

It has been revealed that once the film submission period ends (Nov. 24 this year), an eligibility committee comprising current Globes voters (the quantity and names are kept private) evaluates every submission for “potential misclassification issues.” If found, they “may contact the studio … to discuss those issues and to resolve them informally.” Eventually, the eligibility committee meets with a review committee to discuss any outstanding concerns, and those committees — or at least members of them who have seen a film in question — vote to determine if a change is necessary; two-thirds must favor a change for one to occur.

In a recent development, why do people try to game the Globes categories? Because the nationally telecast Globes ceremony provides the biggest spotlight for awards contenders before Oscar nominations voting (the 2027 Globes will take place Jan. 10, and Oscar nomination voting starts the next morning), making it highly valuable for a film or individual to be represented at the ceremony as a nominee or, better still, a winner.

There usually are fewer standout musicals and comedies than dramas, meaning it’s often easier to land a nom or win if a drama can pass as a musical/comedy. (This year’s aforementioned musical/comedy submissions surely wanted to get out of the way of The Odyssey.) Another motivation: Studios with multiple films prefer to not have them pitted against one another. (A24 probably wants Club Kid to compete as a drama because it already has The Invite and The Debut up for best musical/comedy, just as Neon probably wants Artificial to compete as a comedy because it already has All of a Sudden, Fjord and Paper Tiger up for best drama.).

It remains to be seen whether the Globes’ eligibility committee will overturn some of this year’s submissions. (Reports suggest it already rejected Michael as a musical/comedy.).

Industry observers note that moving forward, it would make everyone’s life easier if the Globes consolidated its genre-specific categories — picture, actor and actress — into single categories with 12 slots rather than divided categories with six each. Or, if the Globes prefers to continue to have multiple categories for each in order to yield twice as many winners, it might consider retaining the “drama” label for one but changing the other to “genre,” which would better describe recent musical/comedy nominees like Poor Things, The Substance and Bugonia.

#12930. Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured

Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, an independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity.
  • Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image shows the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away.
  • According to recent reports, the image of this black hole, designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, an independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity. That, in turn, verifies Einstein's greatest theory, general relativity, which first predicted the existence of black holes and what their immediate surroundings would look like.

Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image shows the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away.

According to recent reports, the image of this black hole, designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement. That may lead to the question: why did it need verifying at all?

Team leader and researcher with Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Samuel Lai explained why capturing the image of a distant black hole is so tricky.

"It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the moon," Lai mentioned in a statement sent to Space.com via email.

According to recent reports, lai and his small Australian team developed advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to capture information about the black hole's structure and filter out interference resulting from the fact that the EHT was viewing M87* from within our planet's atmosphere. The machine-learning technique called GenDIReCT also accounted for biases introduced by combining telescopes to create an Earth-sized interferometer. "When we applied it to the original EHT dataset, we found a black hole almost identical in size and shape as the historic EHT image. Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data," Lai continued. "This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an notable step in the scientific process.".

This could settle the questions of just how the final image of M87* was influenced by both atmospheric effects and the processing methods needed to reconstruct pictures from telescope data.

That's not just good news for the EHT; it's good news for Einstein.

Recent findings suggest that einstein published his theory of general relativity in 1915, completely reshaping how we think of gravity. General relativity suggested that objects with mass curve the very fabric of space and time, united as a single entity called spacetime. Gravity arises from that curvature.

The greater the mass, the more extreme the curvature and thus the greater the gravitational influence of that object. Taking this to its extreme, scientist Karl Schwarzschild came up with a solution to the equations of general relativity that suggested an infinitesimal region with infinite mass, resulting in unrestrained curvature, a singularity. Around this would be a spherical boundary at which not even light has the velocity needed to escape this region. Referred to as the Schwarzschild radius, that boundary became known as the event horizon of a black hole. The singularity, its heart. Black holes were born in 1915, decades before their discovery and over a century before the EHT saw one.

General relativity also predicted what the region around the event horizon would look like. A ring of superheated glowing plasma with the shadow of the black hole falling on it.When scientists first saw the image of M87* they were astounded at how close it reflected predictions made by general relativity, thus confirming the the theory once again. This verification further solidifies that development.

Verifying the EHT's image of M87* could lead to the CSIRO-developed technique being applied to some more "down-to-Earth" uses such as improving medical imaging and mapping earthquakes.

"Independent validation is at the heart of the scientific process, and it is especially valuable for results as novel as those of the EHT. It is extremely gratifying to see that GenDIReCT, an elegant, entirely independent method, recovers the ring structure of M87* across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration’s published results," Laurent Loinard, Director of the EHT Collaboration, noted.

"Studies like this strengthen our confidence in what we have learned about black holes, and enrich the toolkit available to the whole community.".

The team's research was published on Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature.

He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism.
  • The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
  • The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism revealed remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies.

Industry observers note that to explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

Recent findings suggest that movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies.".

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages.

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

Recent findings suggest that at first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

People with autism showed substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

This increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research.

The results raise vital questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Industry observers note that traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?".

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support.".

It has been revealed that the researchers now plan to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since Rockstar released previews of Grand Theft Auto VI this summer, social media has buzzed about the relationship system at the heart of the game.
  • Now that GTA 6 is out, discussion of the latter has resurfaced on X:.
  • But can making small gestures of affection in a video game actually teach players anything about being a better partner IRL?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since Rockstar released previews of Grand Theft Auto VI this summer, social media has buzzed about the relationship system at the heart of the game. While some critics jumped to say that playing GTA 6 is cheating on your significant other, others speculated that playing the game might actually make players better at IRL connections — especially considering that young adults have less experience.

Now that GTA 6 is out, discussion of the latter has resurfaced on X:.

But can making small gestures of affection in a video game actually teach players anything about being a better partner IRL? To answer that question, I reached out to sex and couples therapist Ilana Grines, whom I previously spoke to about whether playing the game is cheating.

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections.

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups.

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups.

Pure — best for anonymous hookups.

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity.

"We have to be really careful about what we're claiming that video games can actually do for us," Grines said. It's useful when individuals are exposed to behaviors that are typically associated with relationship satisfaction as a whole — like spending time together — but, she said, "your girlfriend doesn't have a meter on her forehead that increased the more you...show her attention.".

Recent findings suggest that part of the online conversation stems from the relationship between GTA 6 protagonists Jason and Lucia, whose connection develops through the player's actions. While players can choose to keep their relationship platonic, the game still tracks their bond. Holding hands, buying flowers, giving compliments, sending texts, and running errands together (which may or may not involve committing crimes) can all improve their relationship score.

In a recent development, the relationship meter gives players a sense of where Jason and Lucia stand with one another, Mashable's editorial director Eric Miller explained to me, a self-professed non-gamer. While previous GTA games have featured romantic relationships and family dynamics, GTA 6 takes things a step further by allowing players to actively shape the protagonists' relationship. Depending on their actions, Jason and Lucia can be running on empty (1/4), partners in crime (2/4), crazy in love (3/4), or hot together (4/4).

In a recent development, grines is skeptical that simply performing these actions in a game can teach emotional intelligence. "You're literally playing a game when you could be participating in your relationship," Grines continued. That's another line of thinking that's echoed on social media today: That people (mostly men) are doing chores for Lucia instead of their IRL girlfriend.

One of Grines' clients told her that his girlfriend isn't letting him buy the game — but not because of Lucia. It's actually because of the strip club scenes and how realistic the characters look. The girlfriend isn't comfortable with him going to strip clubs in real life, so why would she be comfortable with him going to one in a video game? As in our discussion over whether playing GTA 6 is cheating, Grines noted she's entitled to set a boundary.

Real relationships, of course, are more complicated than any in-game relationship meter can capture. And Grines warns against having unrealistic expectations for how video games can improve romance. While seeing a healthy relationship modeled in front of you can be useful, she said that modeling doesn't always create behavioral change. Being a good boyfriend in the game doesn't factor in a real partner's own preferences, emotions, and agency. (For example, your real girlfriend may hate flowers!).

In a recent development, that doesn't mean GTA 6 can't bring couples closer together. Gaming can be a shared experience, as PCMag's Jordan Minor demonstrated when he played the game with his wife.

It has been revealed that "It's great that people can experiment and they can repeat actions that may improve their relationship satisfaction," she mentioned. "The real test will be if they can take it out of the video game and into their real lives.".

In a recent development, not everyone likes this element of the game. Right-wing (or right-wing adjacent) influencers Asmongold and Clavicular (who was indicted on two rape charges yesterday) expressed their distaste for GTA 6. The former called the game a "cuck simulator" while playing it on stream, and Clavicular said the game is "insanely cucked.".

Then again, GTA 6 is the highest-rated game of all time, so the haters are in the minority.

Anna Iovine is the associate editor of features at Mashable. Previously, as the sex and relationships reporter, she covered topics ranging from dating apps to pelvic pain. Before Mashable, Anna was a social editor at VICE and freelanced for publications such as Slate and the Columbia Journalism Review. Follow her on Instagram.

#12923. The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1185 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy.
  • Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words.
  • The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A latest study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

It has been revealed that "The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," remarked Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy shows up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction.".

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy.

The researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

Sources indicate that to investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about key moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

It has been revealed that the analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language.

Industry observers note that participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Meanness, however, showed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

In a recent development, boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

These differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life.".

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes.

According to recent reports, the researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

According to recent reports, this variation is crucial because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

"People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray remarked. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

It has been revealed that "Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships.".

Sources indicate that like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

Recent findings suggest that this approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment.

Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

Recent findings suggest that "That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict crucial outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's vital to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict.".

Researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

Industry observers note that "If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she remarked. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions.".

Materials provided by University of Mississippi. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

While there are several early parts of the open-world title that are wowing gamers and internet onlookers alike, one key plot point revealed in the first 30 minutes of “GTA 6” gameplay is getting particular praise, as it reveals the impressive lengths Rockstar Games went to keep the twist under wraps through years of intentional marketing and unofficial leaks.

Protagonists Jason Duval (Dylan Rourke) and Lucia Caminos (Manni L. Perez) have a son: Baby “Tommy” Tomas.

It has been revealed that “GTA 6” opens with a flashback to a double-grand-theft-auto meet-cute between Jason and Lucia. He goes to steal a car that she’s already stolen, the cops come and love blooms. Through a montage of their relationship, we see their happy times and things fall apart as Lucia wants to get more involved in some of Jason’s criminal activities and he refuses to bring her along.

According to recent reports, after the two seemingly split, we see Lucia sitting in a restaurant ordering only water when she decides to rob a payday loan shop across the street. She’s still living in their fictional state of Leonida (inspired by Florida), but she’s on her own and hurting for cash after being suspended from her rideshare driver job.

The crime is a bust, and we catch up to Lucia in present day, where she’s in prison for the attempted armed robbery. She’s now up for a house-arrest-type program, and we learn she wants to go live with Jason when she’s out. We also learn that he’s the “father” of her child.

According to recent reports, cut back to the day when Lucia tried to rob the loan shop, and she’s seen screaming about how she needs to go back to the restaurant. It’s then revealed to players that Lucia left her infant son, Tomas, behind in the restaurant across the street and he’s crying, surrounded by restaurant employees while waiting for her to return.

Industry observers note that from here, it’s up to “GTA 6” players to decide how they want Lucia and Jason (who in present day knows he has a son but has still never met him) to live their lives when they reunite upon her release. Tommy is in the custody of Lucia’s aunt, but will he stay that way, depending on how you play?

According to recent reports, the Tomas twist adds an emotional arc to the game that the franchise hasn’t seen before and comes as returning “GTA” players are in a different stage of their lives (many now likely parents) than they were when “GTA 5” came out 13 years ago. It heightens the stakes for a “GTA” player who now has to evaluate their choices beyond the fun of stealing cars and robbing banks.

Official “GTA 6” sales figures have yet to be revealed, though Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick has assured the Rockstar Games’ results are forthcoming, early data from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates more than $2 billion in pre-order sales alone.

The game currently has a 99 score on Metacritic, tying it for the highest-rated video game of all time with 1998’s “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.”.
