General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nasa ↗ Open Full Page

NASA’s Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel.
  • Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday.
  • “Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) Nov. 18.

Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday.

“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” stated Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.”.

Scientists use light to measure the vast distances of space. Light travels at about 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) a second in a vacuum. A ray of sunlight passing Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, about four hours to reach Neptune, and another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1. For comparison, a light-year is 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).

Recent findings suggest that even though the team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, the spacecraft is sending what is called a carrier signal, which typically conveys that data to Earth. Mission engineers used the carrier signal and trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day milestone. They continue to analyze the problem impacting the science and engineering data.

Humanity’s only probes in interstellar space, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Managed by JPL, they were only the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn, and the first to return high-resolution imagery, transforming our understanding of these worlds and their moons. Voyager 2 went on to study the ethereal ice giants, Neptune and Uranus. Both spacecraft continue to measure changes in the Sun’s magnetic field across vast distances.

Recent findings suggest that “Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” stated Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”.

In addition to their suite of scientific instruments, the Voyager probes carry a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph compiling images and sounds from Earth, as a message to any advanced civilization that might one day find it.

“Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward,” said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. “Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.”.

Traveling about 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), Voyager 1 in 2012 became the first spacecraft to leave the heliosphere, the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the Sun that deflects cosmic radiation, and enter interstellar space. Voyager 2, taking a different trajectory, crossed the boundary in 2018.

Industry observers note that “The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere,” noted Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. “One significant surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.”.

Creative engineering solutions have enabled the probes to conserve energy and overcome challenges related to aging hardware, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer on the spacecraft. Earlier this year, engineers successfully turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives — a move not without risk — to help the spacecraft make the most of its 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator. Essentially a nuclear battery, the generator converts heat from decaying plutonium into electricity.

With the plutonium supply continually depleting, both Voyager probes lose about 4 watts of power each year. The latest energy-saving effort is expected to provide enough power for both spacecraft to keep their current suite of science instruments operating until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer.

As with all NASA spacecraft that venture to and beyond the Moon, communication between Earth and the Voyager probes is managed by the agency’s Deep Space Network, large antennas located at three facilities around the world.

Industry observers note that “We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. “Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity’s silent ambassador to the stars.”.

#12865. Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1441 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that deep beneath the ocean's surface, strange, translucent creatures known as sea pigs crawl across the seafloor.
  • According to recent reports, the researchers identified the bacterium, which they named Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola, and used fluorescence imaging to pinpoint its location inside sea pig tissues.
  • According to recent reports, sea lions, seahorses, and sea cows may be familiar marine animals, but sea pigs are considerably less well known.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that deep beneath the ocean's surface, strange, translucent creatures known as sea pigs crawl across the seafloor. Now, researchers at the University of Tokyo have discovered that these unusual animals are hiding something even stranger beneath their "skin." Living within their body walls is a previously unknown bacterium with an extraordinarily small genome and a surprising collection of genes responsible for producing enormous proteins.

According to recent reports, the researchers identified the bacterium, which they named Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola, and used fluorescence imaging to pinpoint its location inside sea pig tissues. Genetic analysis revealed that its genome contains just 649,000 DNA bases, yet more than a quarter of its genetic material is devoted to producing groups of proteins associated with the bacterial surface. Some of these "giant" proteins contain more than 5,000 amino acids and may help the bacteria interact with their hosts or form clusters (clustering into groups). The discovery offers latest insights into how bacteria adapt to living in close association with other organisms and which biological functions they retain as they become increasingly dependent on their hosts.

Meet the Strange Sea Pigs of the Deep Ocean.

According to recent reports, sea lions, seahorses, and sea cows may be familiar marine animals, but sea pigs are considerably less well known. These small, gelatinous creatures are actually a type of sea cucumber that inhabits the deep ocean. Using numerous tube-shaped feet, they slowly travel across the seafloor, gathering decaying organic material and delivering it to their mouths with specialized tentacles.

Despite their unusual appearance, sea pigs perform important work in the deep-sea ecosystem. By consuming dead organic matter, they help recycle nutrients that support other marine life. Their soft, seemingly vulnerable bodies also provide an unexpected benefit to other animals. Young king crabs have been observed using sea pigs as shelter from predators.

Many aspects of sea pig biology, however, remain mysterious. Researchers still do not know how long these animals live or precisely why they have long, waving projections resembling antennae on their heads. Another notable unanswered question concerns the bacteria that inhabit the layers beneath their outer surfaces.

It has been revealed that sea pigs belong to a group of marine invertebrates called echinoderms (marine invertebrates including sea cucumbers and sea stars). Like other members of this group, they can harbor bacteria beneath their outer body covering. Scientists are particularly interested in understanding how these microorganisms interact with their hosts and how such relationships evolved. This research is also ecologically crucial because sea cucumbers make up more than 90% of the biomass of large seafloor animals in some deep-ocean environments.

Recent findings suggest that "Taxonomic and genomic information about these body-wall inhabiting bacteria is scarce, and very few studies of deep-sea species have linked this information to the bacteria's location within host tissues," remarked Yu Yoshida, a Ph.D. student at the University of Tokyo's Graduate School of Frontier Sciences and a lead author of the study.

Scientists Discover a Dominant Bacterium Beneath Sea Pig Skin.

To investigate these hidden microorganisms, researchers from several Japanese institutions, including the University of Tokyo, examined eight sea pigs collected during deep-sea research expeditions.

The team extracted DNA from different tissues to identify the bacteria present throughout the animals' bodies. They also reconstructed the genomes of the most abundant bacterial groups, allowing them to investigate their genetic characteristics. Finally, they used fluorescence imaging, a technique that makes selected biological structures visible through fluorescent signals, to determine precisely where the bacteria lived within the sea pig tissues.

The results revealed that one particular bacterium was remarkably abundant in the animals' body walls.

"What we found was that in body-wall samples from the three sea pig species, one bacterium accounted for more than 70% of bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequences (a genetic marker used in identifying bacteria), so it truly dominated the body wall," explained Yoshida.

Further investigation demonstrated that this dominant bacterium belongs to a broader group of microorganisms known to live in close association with marine invertebrates. However, its genetic characteristics differ substantially from those of previously identified members of that group.

Because of these differences, the researchers have proposed recognizing Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola as a new bacterial genus and species.

A Tiny Genome Packed With Giant Proteins.

One of the most surprising findings emerged when the scientists examined the bacterium's DNA. Its genome was exceptionally compact, containing only 649,000 bases, the chemical units that make up genetic material.

By comparison, the genome of Escherichia coli, a widely studied bacterium commonly found in the intestines of humans and other animals, is roughly seven times larger.

It has been revealed that "The complete genome was very small, only 649,000 bases. By comparison, the E. coli genome is approximately seven times larger. However, we were more surprised by the composition. Genes for some of the energy-generating pathways (used for breaking down nutrients and generating energy) which are commonly found in bacteria were not detected," explained Yoshida.

The absence of genes involved in certain energy-producing processes suggests that the bacterium may have lost some of the biological machinery that many other bacteria use to survive independently.

Yet even more remarkable was how much of its limited genetic material was devoted to proteins associated with its surface.

"Meanwhile, genes for encoding surface-associated protein groups (that is, DNA with the blueprints for building specific proteins on cell surfaces) accounted for 27.6% of the entire genome. This included genes for proteins exceeding 5,000 amino acids. As bacterial proteins average about 300 amino acids in length, 5,000 is exceptionally long. This offers us important clues as to which functions are retained in bacteria which live in close association with their host.".

Proteins are built from chains of amino acids, and their structures help determine the jobs they perform. The unusually large proteins identified in this bacterium could be involved in interactions with sea pig tissues or in helping bacterial cells stick together. Their exact functions remain unknown.

The discovery suggests that, as the bacterium evolved to depend more heavily on its host, it may have retained certain specialized capabilities while losing genes needed for other essential processes.

What Do Sea Pigs Gain From These Mysterious Bacteria?

The bacterium's unusually reduced genome offers an important clue about its lifestyle. Researchers believe Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola relies extensively on its sea pig host to obtain substances it cannot adequately produce for itself.

These include amino acids, which are necessary for building proteins, along with nucleic acid precursors, lipids, and mineral nutrients. Nucleic acid precursors are the molecular building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, while lipids are notable components of cell membranes and other cellular structures.

Because the bacterium lacks some of the genes needed to produce or process essential compounds independently, living within the sea pig's tissues may provide access to resources required for its survival.

Industry observers note that what remains unclear is whether the relationship also benefits the sea pig. One possibility is that the bacteria help defend their hosts against pathogens, potentially offering protection from disease-causing microorganisms. However, the researchers emphasize that this potential benefit has not yet been demonstrated.

Recent findings suggest that understanding why this particular bacterium becomes so abundant in sea pig body walls is another major question. Scientists also hope to determine what its unusually large surface proteins do, how it competes with other microorganisms, and whether its presence changes the health or biology of its host.

Industry observers note that "We would really like to understand how this bacterium could become so dominant in the body wall, the functions of the giant surface proteins, what competition it faces from other bacteria, and of course the effects on the host," mentioned Yoshida. "More broadly, further investigation could provide fundamental insights into how bacteria colonize hosts and adopt a host-dependent lifestyle.".

The findings highlight how much remains to be discovered about life in the deep ocean. By investigating the microscopic organisms living within these unusual animals, scientists hope to better understand the evolutionary processes that allow bacteria to form intimate, long-lasting relationships with their hosts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Nov. 18 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi.

Test teams fired the developmental engine for the planned duration of three minutes and 20 seconds (200 seconds).

While this developmental engine will not be used in flight, the hot fire test provides NASA and NASA’s prime contractor L3Harris Technologies with the capability to capture critical data to improve engine performance and reliability for future Artemis missions.

Recent findings suggest that for the Artemis IV Moon landing mission in 2028, the SLS rocket will launch astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This mission will be a key step in the agency’s broader goals to explore the lunar South Pole, establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface, and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

For each Artemis mission, four RS-25 engines produce up to 2 million pounds of combined thrust to help launch the SLS rocket.

Recent findings suggest that all RS-25 engines are tested and proven flightworthy at NASA Stennis prior to use. Tests are conducted by a team of operators from NASA, L3Harris, and Nova Space Solutions.
